paragraphs: Regularized learning combines a measure of prediction error with a penalty on the chosen model. This paper asks when solutions to such problems reliably approach the desired population solution as more data become available. It organizes the analysis around three properties: scaled uniform convergence, super-norm regularization, and norm-loss monotonicity. Together, these define the family of problems covered by the framework.

The guarantees address several distinct kinds of success. Loss consistency concerns predictive performance, while norm consistency concerns convergence measured through a norm. Sparsistency means recovering which components belong in the model, and sign consistency concerns recovering their signs. The framework gathers existing guarantees into one formulation and extends them to additional settings.

Its breadth comes from avoiding several assumptions often used in separate analyses. Many results allow unbounded hypothesis classes or samples that are not identically distributed. The loss and regularizer need not be bounded, convex, or smooth, and empirical optimization may be approximate. These conclusions remain conditional on the framework’s defining properties; the paper does not claim consistency for arbitrary regularized learning problems.
icml-2014-a-unified-framework-for-consis.tldr: A common framework establishes several forms of consistency for regularized learning under broad, explicitly defined conditions.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter optimization can find strong settings without explaining why those settings work. This paper addresses the resulting interpretability gap: which hyperparameters account for performance differences, and which matter through their interactions? Its approach reuses the observations already collected by Bayesian optimization, extracting additional insight from an existing search.

The method fits a random forest that predicts performance from hyperparameter settings. A new linear-time algorithm computes marginal predictions, which summarize the model’s predictions while averaging over other settings. These summaries feed into functional ANOVA, a framework that separates performance variation into contributions associated with individual hyperparameters and combinations of them. This makes interactions part of the analysis rather than treating every setting independently.

Experiments cover machine learning frameworks and solvers for combinatorial problems. In the studied cases, a small number of hyperparameters account for most performance variation, even when the full configuration space has many dimensions. This finding helps explain where tuning effort matters in those applications. The contribution is both computational and interpretive: efficient calculations turn optimization records into a structured account of performance sensitivity.
icml-2014-an-efficient-approach-for-asse.tldr: Random forest marginals and functional ANOVA reveal which hyperparameters and interactions explain performance variation using existing optimization data.

paragraphs: Manifold learning seeks a compact representation of data originally described by many coordinates. Conventional geometric viewpoints examine either the original data space or the space containing the resulting embedding. This paper develops a third viewpoint: a space whose elements are entire models, with each model representing a particular collection of points.

Under this interpretation, the input dataset and the output embedding are both models. Learning becomes a trajectory through intermediate models, so the mathematical object of interest is the transformation between complete configurations. The authors derive a unique, closed-form semi-Riemannian metric for this hypothesis space using the information geometry of probability distributions. That metric supplies the geometric structure for studying these transformations.

The framework also connects the volume of a continuous region in model space with an amount of information. Such measurements provide definitions of model complexity and embedding quality within the same theory. The contribution is therefore a unifying mathematical perspective: it relates the geometry of representations, their information content, and the process of moving from data to an embedding.
icml-2014-an-information-geometry-of-sta.tldr: The paper views manifold learning as movement through a geometrically defined space of models, linking embedding quality and complexity to information.

paragraphs: Large collaborative information systems contain more activity than researchers can thoroughly inspect by hand. This makes it difficult to study manipulation, information trustworthiness, and possible bias. The paper introduces a statistical framework that classifies points of view from user interactions, providing an automated way to investigate these questions at Web scale.

The central move is to use interactions as evidence about viewpoint. The framework is intended for a variety of collective intelligence processes, and the authors demonstrate its effectiveness on synthetic data and Wikipedia interactions. This connects the statistical task of identifying viewpoints with the practical task of understanding how participants relate to one another in a large collaborative setting.

The authors also construct a joint model of topics and points of view using the entire history of English Wikipedia. They show how this model can flag potentially biased articles and produce high-level visualizations of user interactions. Those outputs support investigation: identifying potential bias does not itself establish that an article is biased or that a participant is manipulating information.
icml-2014-automated-inference-of-point-o.tldr: A scalable statistical framework infers viewpoints from user interactions and helps identify potentially biased content in collaborative systems.

paragraphs: Random feature maps approximate kernel computations by representing data with a finite collection of features. This paper identifies a weakness in earlier polynomial-kernel approximations: their maps are rank deficient. In effect, the generated features do not fully use the representational capacity of the space allocated to them, limiting how efficiently they approximate the kernel.

The proposed compact random feature maps, called CRAFTMaps, address that wasted capacity. The aim is to represent polynomial kernels more concisely while improving reconstruction accuracy. The authors prove error bounds supporting better kernel reconstruction than previous approximation schemes. They also explain how structured random matrices can generate the maps efficiently, connecting the approximation result with a practical computation method.

The paper carries the feature construction through to learning by presenting a single-pass algorithm for nonlinear multiclass classification. Experiments on several standard datasets produce results competitive with leading methods. The findings support two related contributions: a more effective use of a finite feature space and an efficient route from those features to a working classifier.
icml-2014-compact-random-feature-maps-82.tldr: CRAFTMaps improve polynomial-kernel approximation by using feature-space capacity more effectively and supporting efficient single-pass classification.

paragraphs: Concentration inequalities describe how tightly random quantities stay near their typical values. This paper extends McDiarmid’s inequality to metric spaces whose diameter is unbounded. The key replacement is a distribution-dependent quantity called the subgaussian diameter, which captures relevant probabilistic behavior even when the largest possible distance cannot provide a finite bound.

This approach yields useful bounds independent of dimension in some cases where an earlier method based on weakly difference-bounded functions does not. The paper then applies the concentration result to algorithmic stability, which studies how changes in training data affect a learning algorithm. The authors describe their result as apparently the first generalization bound in this setting that permits unbounded loss functions, and derive a risk bound for some regularized metric regression algorithms.

Two extensions broaden the framework further. One replaces independence with an appropriate strong-mixing condition, allowing certain forms of dependence. The other extends the technique beyond subgaussian behavior to other Orlicz norms. The contribution is a way to obtain informative probabilistic guarantees through distributional control rather than a finite worst-case diameter.
icml-2014-concentration-in-unbounded-met.tldr: A distribution-sensitive extension of McDiarmid’s inequality enables stability-based learning guarantees for certain unbounded losses.

paragraphs: Total least squares handles regression when both inputs and outputs contain measurement errors. Its ordinary form can be solved with singular value decomposition when all variables have equally strong, uncorrelated Gaussian noise. The paper targets more realistic settings, including unequal noise levels, structured errors, and large outliers that call for robust error measures.

The authors develop convex relaxation approaches for structured total least squares. A central finding is that the plain nuclear-norm relaxation can introduce large approximation errors in this setting. A reweighted nuclear-norm approach is much more effective in their theoretical and experimental analysis, and achieves higher accuracy than popular nonconvex solvers on challenging problems. The choice of relaxation therefore materially affects the quality of the resulting estimate.

The paper also describes a fast solution based on an augmented Lagrangian formulation. Its biological application uses population-average measurements to infer expression levels specific to cell types and physiological states, quantities that are difficult to measure directly. This illustrates why explicitly accommodating measurement structure matters: the observed averages must support inference about more specific underlying quantities.
icml-2014-convex-total-least-squares-022.tldr: Reweighted nuclear-norm methods improve structured total least squares for regression with realistic errors in both inputs and outputs.

paragraphs: The paper predicts protein secondary structure by assigning a structural state to each amino-acid residue. Its approach extends generative stochastic networks to supervised learning, using deep hierarchical representations to inform these local predictions. The supervised network learns a Markov chain that samples from a conditional distribution, connecting the generative modeling mechanism to the prediction task.

To handle full protein sequences containing hundreds of amino acids, the authors introduce a convolutional architecture. This supports efficient learning across multiple representation layers. The architecture uses both lower-level and higher-level learned representations when predicting the structured residue labels, so the final local decisions can draw on several levels of information within the model.

Training and evaluation use separate sets of non-homologous proteins with less than 30% sequence identity. On CB513, the model achieves 66.4% Q8 accuracy, compared with the previously reported best result of 64.9% cited in the abstract. This provides empirical support for the supervised convolutional GSN on the stated prediction task, while the sequence separation is an important feature of the reported evaluation.
icml-2014-deep-supervised-and-convolutio.tldr: A supervised convolutional generative stochastic network improves reported protein secondary-structure prediction by combining multiple levels of learned representation.

paragraphs: Particle-based methods offer a flexible way to approximate distributions, but a large state space can leave their representation sparse. Beam search and sequential Monte Carlo may then cover too little of the space to represent uncertainty adequately. This paper addresses that coverage problem by changing what a particle stands for.

An abstract particle represents an entire region of the state space. The method combines these regional representations into a hierarchy, producing a decomposition designed to remain compact while retaining flexibility. Representing regions changes how the available particles cover possible states: the approximation can describe broader portions of the space through a structured collection of abstractions.

The authors evaluate the filtering method on text reconstruction and multiple-object tracking. It empirically outperforms both beam search and sequential Monte Carlo on these tasks. These findings support the usefulness of the regional representation in two distinct applications. The central contribution is the combination of abstract particles with a hierarchical decomposition, addressing inadequate coverage through the organization of the approximate distribution itself.
icml-2014-filtering-with-abstract-partic.tldr: Hierarchically organized particles that represent whole regions improve filtering performance on text reconstruction and multiple-object tracking.

paragraphs: Learning distances on a data manifold often begins by embedding that manifold in Euclidean space. Such a transformation may fail to preserve the desired distances when the original geometry is not Euclidean. This paper develops an approach that learns the distance function directly on the manifold, keeping the original geometry central to the procedure.

The authors first characterize the distance function through its gradient field, which describes its local direction of change. This motivates a two-stage strategy: learn the field, then recover a distance function consistent with it. The algorithm starts with the gradient of a local distance function and transports this initial vector field across the manifold using heat flow on vector fields.

After normalizing the transported field, the method obtains the geodesic distance function by requiring its gradient to stay close to that field. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate the algorithm’s effectiveness. The contribution links a theoretical characterization to a concrete construction: local directional information is spread over the manifold and then used to recover distances.
icml-2014-geodesic-distance-function-lea.tldr: The method learns geodesic distances directly on a manifold by spreading a local gradient field with heat flow.

paragraphs: Hard Thresholding Pursuit is a greedy iterative method for finding sparse solutions to underdetermined linear systems. This paper extends that idea beyond its compressed-sensing setting to a broader class of convex optimization problems with explicit sparsity constraints. The objective is to retain the method’s strong convergence and estimation properties across more learning tasks.

The proposed algorithm alternates between a standard gradient-descent update and hard truncation. The gradient step improves the objective, while truncation limits how many components remain active in the solution. The paper considers versions with and without debiasing, providing variants of this basic update pattern. This gives a direct algorithmic mechanism for combining objective improvement with sparse selection.

The authors prove convergence-rate and parameter-estimation guarantees analogous to those established for the original method. They also report numerical advantages over leading greedy selection approaches on sparse logistic regression and sparse support vector machines. The theoretical results support the generalization of the pursuit framework, while the experiments demonstrate its usefulness for the two stated learning applications.
icml-2014-gradient-hard-thresholding-pur.tldr: Gradient Hard Thresholding Pursuit extends sparse greedy optimization to convex learning objectives with convergence and estimation guarantees.

paragraphs: Rejected updates in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo can waste function evaluations and contribute to random-walk behavior. This paper introduces a method that largely avoids those rejections. When a situation would ordinarily cause rejection, it continues computing a longer trajectory until it reaches a new state that can be accepted.

The mathematical change concerns the conditions imposed on the Markov chain. The transitions satisfy the fixed-point equation, which preserves the intended stationary distribution, without satisfying detailed balance. This allows the sampler to retain the required distributional behavior while using transitions that need not obey the stronger balance condition. The extended trajectory is therefore part of a deliberately constructed sampling rule.

On three test problems, the authors demonstrate an improvement in mixing time by more than a factor of two. This indicates that the modified chain explores its target distribution more effectively in those experiments. The paper also provides Python and MATLAB implementations. Its main contribution is a concrete way to reduce rejection-related waste while maintaining the fixed-point requirement needed for the sampler.
icml-2014-hamiltonian-monte-carlo-withou.tldr: An HMC variant replaces many rejections with longer trajectories and improves mixing by more than twofold on three test problems.

paragraphs: Heavy-tailed data challenge learning guarantees that rely on bounded observations or subgaussian distributions. This paper proposes a computationally efficient estimator for linear regression and other smooth, strongly convex loss-minimization problems. Its loss-approximation guarantees cover general distributions, including heavy-tailed ones, broadening the settings in which efficient estimation has theoretical support.

The main technique generalizes the median-of-means estimator to arbitrary metric spaces. This extends a robust estimation principle beyond settings where estimates are simply numbers. The authors position the method against earlier results that required stronger distributional assumptions, prior knowledge of distributional properties, or estimators without established computational tractability.

A specific regression guarantee allows heavy-tailed responses but requires bounded, well-conditioned covariates in d dimensions. Under those conditions, roughly d log(1/δ) samples, up to additional logarithmic factors, suffice for a constant-factor approximation to optimal loss with probability 1−δ. This sample complexity is minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors. The distinction matters: the stated result controls achieved loss and retains explicit conditions on the covariates.
icml-2014-heavy-tailed-regression-with-a.tldr: A metric-space generalization of median-of-means enables efficient regression with loss guarantees for heavy-tailed data.

paragraphs: Sum-product networks are deep probabilistic representations that permit efficient, exact inference. Learning their structure determines how they express relationships among variables. Earlier SPN learning methods largely used clustering to construct mixtures, representing interactions indirectly through implicit latent variables. Other tractable modeling approaches emphasized direct relationships among observed variables.

The paper introduces ID-SPN, a structure-learning algorithm that combines these two strategies. Its contribution is to bring direct interactions and mixture-based indirect interactions into a single learning approach. This broadens the relationships the structure learner can use while working within the SPN representation, which already encompasses several other families of tractable probabilistic models.

Experiments on 20 benchmark datasets show significantly better accuracy than several leading algorithms for learning SPNs and other tractable models. These results support the value of combining the two forms of interaction in the evaluated settings. The broader lesson is that a structure learner’s choices about how to represent dependence can materially affect accuracy, even within a model family designed to keep inference efficient.
icml-2014-learning-sum-product-networks-.tldr: ID-SPN improves tractable probabilistic learning by combining direct variable relationships with indirect interactions represented through mixtures.

paragraphs: Kernel methods become difficult to scale when they require a large, usually dense matrix of similarities between samples. Low-rank approximation reduces this burden, but the paper identifies an important structural issue: changing the scale parameter of a shift-invariant kernel can move its matrix from a low-rank regime to a block-diagonal regime with no low-rank structure.

Memory Efficient Kernel Approximation, or MEKA, accounts for both low-rank and clustering structure. Its motivation is that an approximation should reflect the organization actually present in the kernel matrix. By considering both forms of structure, the method addresses cases where relying on low rank alone does not capture the matrix effectively.

The authors report improvements in speed, approximation error, and memory use over leading low-rank methods. On MNIST2M, MEKA takes 550 seconds and less than 500 MB on one machine, achieving 0.2313 test RMSE for kernel ridge regression. Standard Nyström takes over 2,700 seconds and over 2 GB for 0.2318 RMSE. This example shows substantially lower resource use with closely comparable predictive error.
icml-2014-memory-efficient-kernel-approx.tldr: MEKA exploits both clustering and low-rank structure to approximate large kernel matrices with lower computational and memory costs.

paragraphs: Joint object matching uses agreement across many objects to improve pairwise correspondences. The paper addresses two challenges together: objects may share only some features, and the supplied matches may contain many errors. Earlier theoretical guarantees could not recover the correct solution beyond a constant corruption fraction, motivating stronger error-correction methods.

The proposed approach encodes a consistent collection of partial maps in a binary semidefinite matrix. Recovery then proceeds in two stages: a spectral technique followed by MatchLift, a parameter-free convex program. This formulation lets the algorithm reason about compatibility across the collection while accommodating partial similarities between individual objects.

Under a randomized model, MatchLift has near-optimal error-correction guarantees and can recover the true maps even when a dominant fraction of input correspondences are randomly corrupted. The random-corruption condition is part of that result; it is not a guarantee against every possible error pattern. Experiments on synthetic and real benchmark datasets support the method’s practical applicability, complementing its theoretical recovery analysis.
icml-2014-near-optimal-joint-object-matc.tldr: MatchLift jointly matches partially similar objects and guarantees recovery under a randomized model even with a dominant fraction of corrupted correspondences.

paragraphs: Training a crowd worker involves choosing examples that help the worker learn a classification rule. This paper treats example selection as an optimization problem, motivated by crowdsourced labeling and online education. It asks how a teacher should choose what a learner sees when learning behavior is uncertain.

The authors model learners as stochastically switching among hypotheses in response to feedback. Their algorithm, STRICT, selects teaching examples by greedily maximizing a submodular surrogate objective. The surrogate gives an efficient objective to optimize within the proposed learner model, connecting individual example choices to the overall teaching task.

The paper proves that the strategy is competitive with the optimal teaching policy. For the special case of linear separators, it also shows that an exponential reduction in error probability can be achieved. Experiments with simulated workers and three real image-annotation tasks on Amazon Mechanical Turk demonstrate effectiveness. Together, these results provide theoretical and empirical support for deliberate example selection, with the formal guarantees tied to the stated modeling framework and special-case conditions.
icml-2014-near-optimally-teaching-the-cr.tldr: STRICT efficiently selects teaching examples and offers guarantees and empirical evidence for improving workers’ classification learning.

paragraphs: A feature-selection path tracks classification accuracy as the fraction of retained features changes. Computing it through repeated multiple-kernel learning can be expensive because many separate optimization problems must be solved. This paper develops a way to follow the path systematically as the regularization parameter p moves toward one.

The authors conjecture that, for certain formulations, the optimal number of selected features decreases monotonically as p decreases. They prove this for a family based on kernel target alignment and establish threshold-dependent monotonic behavior of feature weights. These properties support a path-following algorithm that can set some weights directly to zero over potentially large parameter intervals, reducing optimization work while providing approximation guarantees.

Experiments report classification accuracies up to 10% higher than the stated comparison methods and substantial training-time reductions. The algorithm generates a complete path for datasets with 100,000 features in about half an hour on standard hardware. The result connects a proved property of the specified formulations to a practical reduction in the cost of exploring feature subsets.
icml-2014-on-p-norm-path-following-in-mu.tldr: Monotonicity results for certain multiple-kernel formulations enable efficient feature-selection paths with approximation guarantees.

paragraphs: Matrix completion fills in missing entries by exploiting a low-rank structure. Although useful in applications such as collaborative filtering and image inpainting, many existing methods struggle at large scale because of singular value decomposition costs. This paper develops a scalable approach by extending orthogonal matching pursuit from vectors to matrices.

At each iteration, the algorithm examines the current approximation residual and constructs a rank-one matrix from its top singular-vector pair. It then updates the weights of the rank-one matrices collected so far. A further weight-update rule reduces time and storage requirements, making the accumulated representation more practical for large matrices.

The authors establish linear convergence, attributing the fast rate to the construction of the matrix bases and estimation of their weights. Evaluations on multiple large real-world datasets show much greater efficiency than leading matrix-completion algorithms while maintaining similar or better prediction performance. The contribution joins a greedy matrix representation with an efficient updating procedure, giving both a convergence result and empirical evidence of scalability.
icml-2014-rank-one-matrix-pursuit-for-ma.tldr: A greedy rank-one pursuit algorithm completes large matrices efficiently while providing linear convergence and competitive prediction performance.

paragraphs: In a dueling bandit problem, a learner receives relative feedback about two choices rather than an individual reward for each choice. The challenge is to use these comparisons to make increasingly good selections. This paper adapts Upper Confidence Bound to that pairwise-feedback setting, retaining a confidence-based approach to choosing what to compare.

The method estimates pairwise winning probabilities and uses them to identify a promising arm. It then applies Upper Confidence Bound with that winner as a benchmark. This creates a way to organize further comparisons around a candidate supported by the observed relative outcomes, connecting uncertainty about pairs to the selection process.

For a very general class of dueling bandit problems, the authors prove a finite-time regret bound of order O(K log t), matching an existing lower bound. Here K is the number of arms and t is the time horizon. Experiments using real information-retrieval data show substantial gains over leading methods. The theoretical result characterizes cumulative decision cost, while the experiments demonstrate effectiveness in the stated application.
icml-2014-relative-upper-confidence-boun.tldr: Relative Upper Confidence Bound learns from pairwise comparisons and achieves a matching O(K log t) regret bound for a broad problem class.

paragraphs: Robust principal component analysis seeks useful underlying structure in data affected by noise. The original formulation assumes sparse noise and measures its error with an L1 norm. This paper argues that practical noise can have a more complicated distribution, making a single fixed norm an inadequate model for some datasets.

The authors propose a Bayesian generative formulation that represents noise with a mixture of Gaussians. Because such mixtures can approximate continuous distributions, the model can accommodate a broad range of noise forms, including Gaussian, Laplacian, sparse noise, and combinations of these. The method therefore makes the noise distribution a flexible part of the model.

Inference uses a variational Bayes algorithm, with recursive closed-form updates for all involved parameters. Experiments on synthetic data, face modeling, and background subtraction demonstrate the approach’s advantages. These findings support the practical value of adapting the noise representation in the tested settings. The central contribution combines that flexibility with an explicit inference procedure, rather than leaving a richer noise model without a computational method.
icml-2014-robust-principal-component-ana.tldr: A Bayesian RPCA model uses a Gaussian mixture to accommodate varied noise distributions and supports closed-form variational updates.

paragraphs: Maximum a posteriori inference seeks the most probable assignment in a probabilistic model. For discrete Markov random fields on general graphs, this problem is NP-hard. The paper introduces a semidefinite relaxation, called SDR, to estimate the assignment and focuses on making this approach computationally practical for large problems.

Its solver, SDPAD-LR, is an accelerated variant of the alternating direction method of multipliers. It exploits the special structure of the proposed relaxation. The authors report solving grid-graph problems with hundreds of thousands of variables, each having multiple states. Compared with previous semidefinite-programming solvers, it reaches comparable accuracy with substantially improved scalability.

Evaluations include the OPENGM2 and PIC benchmarks. For a broad class of problems, the method produces better MAP assignments than leading comparison algorithms. These results challenge the idea that semidefinite relaxation is confined to small instances. The contribution is the pairing of a relaxation with a solver designed around its structure, enabling large-scale approximate inference without claiming to solve general NP-hard MAP inference exactly.
icml-2014-scalable-semidefinite-relaxati.tldr: A structured semidefinite relaxation and accelerated solver make approximate MAP inference practical on large discrete graphical models.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decision-making when choices are nodes in a graph and their expected rewards vary smoothly across neighboring nodes. In the recommendation example, each node is an item and neighboring items have similar expected ratings. The learner must identify highly rated items while limiting the cumulative cost of imperfect recommendations.

The authors aim to avoid regret that scales poorly with the total number of nodes. They introduce an effective dimension to characterize the problem’s relevant complexity and propose two algorithms with linear and sublinear scaling in that dimension. The abstract describes this effective dimension as small in real-world graphs, making it a potentially useful alternative to counting every node separately.

Experiments on a real-world content-recommendation problem show that a useful estimate of preferences over thousands of items can be learned from only tens of node evaluations. This supports the value of the graph structure in that setting. The smoothness assumption is central: the approach relies on neighboring nodes having related expected rewards, allowing observations to inform more than the directly evaluated item.
icml-2014-spectral-bandits-for-smooth-gr.tldr: Graph-smooth bandit algorithms use effective dimension to learn preferences across many items from relatively few evaluations.

paragraphs: Recovering a low-rank tensor means reconstructing a multidimensional array from incomplete measurements. A common convex approach sums the nuclear norms of matrices formed by unfolding the tensor. This paper proves that this sum-of-norms formulation can require substantially more information than the tensor’s structure would otherwise suggest.

For a K-way tensor with side length n and Tucker rank (r, …, r), reliable recovery from Gaussian measurements using that formulation requires on the order of r n^(K−1) observations. An intractable nonconvex formulation needs only O(r^K + nrK). The authors introduce a tractable convex relaxation that succeeds with O(r^floor(K/2) n^ceil(K/2)) observations, partially closing the gap.

The lower bound follows from a broader result about signals possessing several structures at once. Adding separate structure-promoting norms can be significantly suboptimal because the resulting penalty may not exploit those structures jointly. The new tensor formulation demonstrates that designing the regularizer around their combination can reduce sample requirements. Its improvement narrows the gap without claiming to match the intractable formulation’s measurement count.
icml-2014-square-deal-lower-bounds-and-i.tldr: The paper proves weaknesses in sum-of-nuclear-norm tensor recovery and introduces a convex relaxation with improved measurement requirements.

paragraphs: Regularized learning becomes harder to optimize when the penalty has a complex structure. This paper proposes a stochastic dual coordinate ascent method that uses the alternating direction method of multipliers, or ADMM, to handle such regularization. The intended scope includes a wide range of learning problems with structured penalties.

Ordinary ADMM is a batch method, while the proposed update needs only one or a few sample observations per iteration. This combines ADMM’s treatment of complex regularizers with stochastic updates that avoid requiring a full batch at every step. The method also naturally supports mini-batches, and the authors report that these can accelerate convergence.

Under assumptions described as mild, the paper proves exponential convergence. Numerical experiments also show efficient performance, providing empirical support alongside the theoretical rate. The convergence claim is conditional on those assumptions rather than a statement about every possible regularized objective. The main contribution is an optimization method that brings structured regularization and small-sample updates into the same algorithmic framework, with both convergence analysis and practical evaluation.
icml-2014-stochastic-dual-coordinate-asc.tldr: An ADMM-based stochastic dual coordinate method handles complex regularization with small-sample updates and conditional exponential convergence.
